name: ReactJS

beginner.content:
• ReactJS is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces.
• It allows developers to create reusable UI components and manage the state of their applications efficiently.
• ReactJS uses a virtual DOM to optimize rendering performance. When the state of a component changes, React updates the virtual DOM and efficiently updates the real DOM.
• React supports server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG) for improved performance and SEO.
• Frameworks like Next.js make it easy to implement these features.

Fresher Notes

  • React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from small reusable pieces called components.
  • You describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and React updates the page efficiently when the data changes.
  • React uses JSX, a syntax that looks like HTML inside JavaScript.

Worked Example 1

Create a project.

Worked Example 2

Rendering a list from data.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal component.

Practice Exercise 2

State makes it interactive.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

React renders in two phases. The render phase calls your components to produce a tree of React elements (plain objects) and compares it with the previous tree (reconciliation) using type and key to decide what to keep, update or remove. The commit phase applies the minimal DOM changes and runs effects. A state update schedules a new render; React batches several updates into one.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to use React: a plain Vite or Create-style SPA, a framework (Next.js, Remix, Gatsby) with routing and server rendering, React Native for mobile, and libraries on top (React Router, TanStack Query, Redux Toolkit, Zustand). Rendering modes: client, server (SSR), static, and streaming with Suspense.

intermediate.content:
• ReactJS uses a virtual DOM to optimize rendering performance.
• When the state of a component changes, React updates the virtual DOM and efficiently updates the real DOM.
• This approach minimizes the number of direct manipulations to the DOM, resulting in faster updates and improved performance.
• React's reconciliation algorithm compares the new virtual DOM with the previous one and updates only the parts of the real DOM that have changed.
• This makes React applications highly performant, even with complex user interfaces.

expert.content:
• ReactJS supports server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG) for improved performance and SEO.
• Frameworks like Next.js make it easy to implement these features.
• SSR allows React components to be rendered on the server and sent to the client as fully rendered HTML, improving initial load times and SEO.
• SSG generates static HTML files at build time, which can be served directly from a CDN, further improving performance and scalability.

• Next.js is a popular React framework that provides built-in support for SSR and SSG.
• It allows developers to create React applications with minimal configuration while benefiting from improved performance and SEO.
• Next.js also offers features like automatic code splitting, optimized image handling, and API routes, making it a powerful choice for building modern web applications with React.

Mid-Level Notes

  • React is declarative: you write the result for a given state, not the steps to change the DOM.
  • Data flows one way: parents pass props down, children report up with callbacks.
  • React renders to a virtual tree, compares it with the previous one (reconciliation) and applies the minimum DOM changes.

Senior Notes

  • React is a view library; routing, data fetching and state management come from libraries or a framework (Next.js, Remix).
  • Keep components small and pure; side effects belong in effects or event handlers.
  • Performance comes from correct keys, memoization where measured, code splitting and avoiding unnecessary state.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Beginner mistakes: mutating state, missing keys in lists, calling hooks conditionally, doing side effects during render, infinite loops from effects that set their own dependencies, and forgetting that setState is asynchronous. Follow the rules of hooks and keep render pure.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: measure first (React DevTools Profiler). Typical wins: stable keys, splitting components so state changes re-render less, memo/useMemo/useCallback for expensive or frequently re-rendered parts, list virtualization, code splitting and avoiding giant state objects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: data loading with a query library handles caching, loading and error states, so components stay simple and the UI reflects server state.

beginner.content:
What is SPA (Single Page Application)?

• A Single Page Application (SPA) is a web application that loads a single HTML page and dynamically updates content as the user interacts with the application, without refreshing the entire page.


Traditional Web App vs SPA

Feature Traditional App SPA
Page Reload Reloads on every request No full page reload
Speed Slower navigation Faster after initial load
Rendering Server-side Client-side

How SPA Works

  • • Browser loads a single HTML file.
  • • JavaScript framework initializes.
  • • User actions trigger API calls.
  • • Server returns JSON data.
  • • DOM updates dynamically.

Advantages

  • • Better user experience
  • • Fast navigation
  • • Reduced bandwidth usage
  • • Rich interactive UI

Disadvantages

  • • Initial load can be heavy
  • • SEO challenges
  • • Browser compatibility issues (older browsers)
  • • Security concerns if not handled properly

Popular SPA Frameworks

  • • React
  • • Angular
  • • Vue.js

Fresher Notes

  • A single page application (SPA) loads one HTML page and then updates the content with JavaScript instead of loading a new page for each link.
  • Navigation feels instant because only data is fetched and parts of the page change.
  • React with a router (React Router) is a common way to build an SPA.

Worked Example 1

History API navigation.

Worked Example 2

Caching hashed assets.

Practice Exercise 1

Server fallback configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Lazy loaded route.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In an SPA the server returns the same HTML shell for every route. The JavaScript bundle boots, the client router reads location.pathname, renders the matching component tree, and intercepts link clicks to call history.pushState instead of navigating. The back button fires popstate, and the router renders the previous route without a request for HTML.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Build and deploy options: static hosting with fallback to index.html, CDN with long-lived hashed assets, server rendering for SEO-critical pages, prerendering, and hybrid frameworks (Next.js). Routing options: hash routing (works without server fallback), browser history routing (clean URLs).

intermediate.content:
SPA Architecture

• SPA typically follows a Client-Server Architecture.
• The frontend communicates with backend services using REST APIs.


Architecture Flow

  1. • User interacts with UI
  2. • Client-side router handles navigation
  3. • API request sent to backend
  4. • Backend processes and returns JSON
  5. • UI re-renders with updated state

Client-Side Routing

Routing in SPA is handled on the client using libraries like:

  • • React Router
  • • Angular Router
  • • Vue Router

State Management

  • • Component State
  • • Context API
  • • Redux
  • • NgRx (Angular)

Authentication in SPA

  • • JWT (JSON Web Token)
  • • OAuth2
  • • Session-based authentication

SPA vs MPA (Multi Page Application)

  • • SPA: Single HTML page, dynamic updates
  • • MPA: Multiple HTML pages, full reload
codeExamples:
// JWT Token Storage Example
localStorage.setItem("token", response.token);

expert.content:
Advanced SPA Concepts


1. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading

• Improves performance by loading only required components.


2. Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

• Improves SEO and performance by rendering pages on server first. Example: Next.js (React Framework).


3. Progressive Web Applications (PWA)

  • • Offline support
  • • Service workers
  • • Installable apps

4. Performance Optimization

  • • Memoization
  • • Virtual DOM optimization
  • • Debouncing & Throttling
  • • Tree shaking

5. Security Best Practices

  • • Prevent XSS attacks
  • • Secure token storage
  • • HTTPS usage
  • • CSRF protection


Interview Questions

  • • What is SPA and how does it work?
  • • Difference between SPA and MPA?
  • • How does client-side routing work?
  • • How do you handle authentication in SPA?
  • • How to optimize SPA performance?

Mid-Level Notes

  • The browser loads a JavaScript bundle once; the router changes the URL with the History API and renders the matching component.
  • Data comes from APIs (fetch/axios) as JSON.
  • The server must return the same index.html for all app routes (fallback) so deep links and refresh work.

Senior Notes

  • Trade-offs: fast navigation and app-like feel versus slower first load, SEO challenges and more client complexity.
  • Mitigate with code splitting, server-side rendering or static generation (Next.js), and prerendering for SEO.
  • Handle history, scroll restoration, loading and error states, and authentication on the client and server.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no server fallback (404 on refresh), a giant single bundle, relying on client-only rendering for SEO pages, forgetting document titles and focus management on navigation, and storing tokens in localStorage without considering XSS. Use code splitting, SSR for public pages and secure cookies.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

SPA performance: measure Core Web Vitals; split by route, lazy load heavy libraries, preload likely next routes, compress with Brotli, cache hashed assets for a year, and avoid blocking the main thread with large JSON processing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: authentication in an SPA. A protected route component checks the session and redirects to login while preserving the intended URL.

beginner.content:
What is Node.js?

• Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine.
• It allows you to run JavaScript outside the browser.


What is npm?

• npm (Node Package Manager) is a tool that comes with Node.js.
• It is used to install, manage, and update JavaScript packages.


Steps to Install Node.js & npm

  1. • Go to the official Node.js website.
  2. • Download the LTS (Long Term Support) version.
  3. • Run the installer and follow setup instructions.
  4. • Restart your system (if required).

Verify Installation

• Open Command Prompt / Terminal and run:
codeExamples: node -v
npm -v

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside the browser. npm is its package manager.
  • Install Node from nodejs.org (LTS version) and check with node -v and npm -v.
  • React tooling (Vite, Create React App, Next.js) runs on Node and installs libraries with npm.

Worked Example 1

Add and remove packages.

Worked Example 2

Reproducible CI install.

Practice Exercise 1

Check and install.

Practice Exercise 2

package.json scripts.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Node.js is a runtime built on V8 with an event loop and system APIs. npm resolves dependency ranges (semver) from the registry into a tree in node_modules, writes exact resolved versions with integrity hashes into package-lock.json, and runs scripts defined in package.json. Tools like Vite use Node to serve and bundle your code.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: package managers npm, pnpm (content-addressable store, fast and strict), yarn; version managers nvm, fnm, Volta; npx to run tools; workspaces for monorepos; .npmrc for registries; overrides/resolutions to force versions; Corepack to pin the manager.

intermediate.content:
Understanding Node.js Installation Types


1. LTS Version

• Recommended for production applications.
• Stable and supported for a long time.


2. Current Version

• Latest features but may not be fully stable.


Installing on Different Operating Systems

Windows

  • • Download .msi installer
  • • Follow setup wizard
  • • Ensure "Add to PATH" is selected

Mac

  • • Download .pkg installer
  • • Or use Homebrew package manager

Linux

  • • Use package manager (apt, yum)
  • • Or install using Node Version Manager (NVM)

Understanding package.json

• package.json is a configuration file that stores:

  • • Project metadata
  • • Dependencies
  • • Scripts
  • • Version details
codeExamples:
// Initialize a new Node project
npm init

// Install a package
npm install express

// Install as dev dependency
npm install nodemon --save-dev

expert.content:
Advanced Node & npm Concepts


Node Version Manager (NVM)

• NVM allows you to install and manage multiple Node.js versions.
• Useful for working on different projects with different versions.


Global vs Local Package Installation

  • • Global: Available system-wide
  • • Local: Installed inside project folder

Understanding node_modules

• node_modules contains all installed dependencies.
• It should not be committed to Git.


npm Scripts

• You can define custom scripts inside package.json.


npx Command

•npx allows running packages without installing them globally.


Security Best Practices

  • • Use npm audit
  • • Keep dependencies updated
  • • Avoid installing unknown global packages

Environment Variables

• Use .env files to store sensitive information.
codeExamples:
// Install NVM (Mac/Linux)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.5/install.sh | bash

// Run npm audit
npm audit

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • package.json lists dependencies and scripts (npm run dev, npm run build).
  • npm install reads package.json and installs into node_modules; package-lock.json pins exact versions.
  • Use a version manager (nvm, fnm, Volta) to switch Node versions per project.

Senior Notes

  • Commit the lockfile and use npm ci in CI for reproducible installs.
  • Audit dependencies (npm audit), keep them updated and avoid unmaintained packages.
  • Scripts and the engines field document required Node versions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: committing node_modules, ignoring the lockfile, installing global packages that differ per machine, running npm install in CI (use ci), mixing package managers in one repo, and trusting every dependency. Fix with a lockfile, ci, one manager, audits and version pinning.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Install time and disk use: pnpm and caches speed up CI, npm ci with a cache directory is faster, and fewer dependencies mean faster installs and smaller attack surface. Measure bundle size and dependency count.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a reproducible build pipeline pins Node, installs from the lockfile, runs tests and builds, caching the package store between runs.

beginner.content:
What is JSX?

• JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write HTML-like markup directly inside a JavaScript/React file.
• JSX is NOT valid JavaScript on its own — a build tool compiles it away before the browser sees it. Under the modern automatic runtime (React 17+, the default in Vite, CRA 5 and Next.js) it becomes _jsx() imported from react/jsx-runtime, which is why you no longer need import React. The legacy classic transform produced React.createElement(...) instead, and the browser still never sver sees it.
• It exists so a component's structure (what it renders) and logic (how it behaves) can live together in one readable file, instead of separate template/script files.

JSX compiles down to function calls

Embedding JavaScript Expressions

Any valid JavaScript expression can be embedded inside JSX using curly braces {} — variables, function calls, arithmetic, ternaries (but NOT statements like if or for directly).

Fresher Notes

  • JSX lets you write HTML-like markup in JavaScript: <h1>Hello</h1>. It is compiled into function calls.
  • Put JavaScript expressions in curly braces: {name}, {price * qty}.
  • Rules: return one root element (or a fragment <>...</>), close all tags, use className and camelCase attributes.

Worked Example 1

XSS safety.

Worked Example 2

Spreading props.

Practice Exercise 1

Expressions and attributes.

Practice Exercise 2

What JSX compiles to.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A build tool (Babel, SWC, esbuild) compiles JSX into calls to the JSX runtime, producing plain element objects { type, props, key }. Components are functions called by React with a props object. Children become the children prop. Because JSX is just expressions, anything JavaScript can do (map, ternary, function calls) works inside braces.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax options: fragments (<>, keyed <Fragment key>), conditional rendering (&&, ternary, early return), lists with keys, spread props, boolean and null children (render nothing), style objects, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, ref and key special props, TypeScript generics in TSX.

expert.content:
The Core JSX Rules

• Single root element — a component must return one root element (or a <>...</> Fragment to avoid an unnecessary wrapper <div>).
• className, not class — class is a reserved JavaScript keyword, so JSX uses className for the HTML class attribute.
• camelCase event handlers and most attributes — onClick not onclick, tabIndex not tabindex.
• Self-closing tags need the slash — <img />, <br />, even for elements that aren't normally self-closing in HTML.
• Comments use {/* ... */} inside JSX, not <!-- -->.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is JSX required to use React?No — it's optional sugar; you can call React.createElement() directly, but virtually no real codebase does that by hand
Why does a component need a single root element?A function can only return one value; JSX with multiple top-level siblings has no single object to return, so it's a compile error unless wrapped in one parent or a Fragment
Why className instead of class?JSX attributes become JavaScript object properties under the hood, and "class" is a reserved word in JavaScript
Can you put an if statement directly inside JSX curly braces?No — only expressions are allowed inside {}, not statements; use a ternary or move the if logic above the return

Mid-Level Notes

  • Attributes: className, htmlFor, onClick, style={{ color: "red" }}.
  • Conditionals and lists use expressions: {cond && <A />}, {items.map(...)}.
  • Comments inside JSX use {/* comment */}.

Senior Notes

  • JSX is escaped by default, which protects against XSS; dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses it, so sanitize first.
  • JSX compiles to jsx() calls from the runtime; any expression that evaluates to a React element works.
  • Keep markup readable: extract subcomponents instead of deeply nested ternaries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: 0 rendered by {count && <X />} (zero is printed), missing keys, objects as children (error), class instead of className, unclosed tags, and string styles. Use ternaries or Boolean(), arrays of elements, and style objects.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

JSX itself is cheap; cost comes from the number of elements rendered and reconciled. Avoid creating huge element trees on every keystroke, split components so only the changed part re-renders, and virtualize long lists.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a reusable button component that forwards props and refs, supports variants through className and keeps accessibility attributes.

beginner.content:
What is a Component?

• A component is a reusable, self-contained piece of UI — a JavaScript function (or class) that returns JSX describing what should appear on screen.
• Components let you split the UI into independent, reusable pieces and think about each piece in isolation.
• React has two ways to write a component: functional (a plain function) and class-based (extends React.Component).

Class Components (Legacy, Still Asked in Interviews)

Before React 16.8 introduced Hooks, class components were the only way to have local state and lifecycle methods. They're less common in new code today, but still appear in older codebases and interview questions.

Fresher Notes

  • A component is a reusable piece of UI. Today most components are functions that return JSX; class components are the older style.
  • Component names start with a capital letter: <ProductCard />.
  • Components receive props and can hold state with hooks.

Worked Example 1

Bug: component defined inside another.

Worked Example 2

Memoized child.

Practice Exercise 1

Function vs class component.

Practice Exercise 2

Composition with children.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Each component call is an independent unit of rendering with its own hook state, kept by React in a fiber tree. The fiber is identified by its position in the tree and its type (and key). If the type and position match between renders, state is preserved; if they differ, React unmounts the old component and mounts a new one. Rendering a component means calling the function again.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: presentational and container components, custom hooks to share logic, compound components (Tabs with Tab), render props, higher-order components, controlled vs uncontrolled components, error boundaries (class), portals, Suspense and lazy components, and context providers.

expert.content:
Why Functional Components + Hooks Won

• Class components need this binding gymnastics (this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)), which is a common source of bugs for beginners.
• Hooks (introduced React 16.8, 2019) let functional components have state and lifecycle behavior WITHOUT classes — see the State/useState and useEffect topics.
• Functional components are generally shorter, easier to test, and easier to compose (custom hooks let you share stateful logic between components — something class components can't do cleanly).
• The React team's own official guidance and nearly all new documentation/tutorials now default to functional components.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a React component, fundamentally?A function (or class) that accepts props and returns JSX describing part of the UI
Are class components deprecated?Not officially removed, but functional components with Hooks are the recommended modern approach for all new code
Why do class components need method binding in the constructor?Regular methods don't automatically bind "this" to the class instance in JavaScript, so event handlers lose their "this" context unless explicitly bound
Can a functional component have state?Yes, via the useState Hook — this is exactly what made functional components a full replacement for class components

Mid-Level Notes

  • Functional components with hooks are the standard; class components remain supported but are rarely written now.
  • Split UI into small components: each does one job and can be reused and tested.
  • Components must be pure during render: same props and state give the same JSX, without side effects.

Senior Notes

  • Container versus presentational patterns, custom hooks for shared logic, and composition with children beat deep inheritance.
  • Do not define components inside other components (they are recreated each render and lose state).
  • Use React.memo, useMemo and useCallback only where profiling shows a benefit.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: components that fetch and render and format everything (hard to test), mutating props, derived state copied from props (gets out of sync), deeply nested conditionals, and components defined inside components. Split by responsibility and derive instead of copying.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Re-render cost: a state change re-renders the component and its children. Co-locate state, split components, memoize expensive children and use stable props. Verify with the Profiler instead of guessing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a design system. Small, consistent, accessible components (Button, Input, Modal, Table) used across features, with props for variants and tests for behaviour.

beginner.content:
What are Props?

• Props (short for "properties") are how a parent component passes data DOWN to a child component.
• Props are read-only — a child component must never modify the props it receives; React relies on this to keep data flow predictable ("one-way data flow").
• Props are passed like HTML attributes, and received by the child as a single object argument (conventionally named props).

Destructuring Props

Instead of writing props.name, props.age everywhere, it's common to destructure props right in the function signature for cleaner code.

Fresher Notes

  • Props are inputs to a component, passed like attributes: <Product name="Pen" price={10} />.
  • A component reads them from its parameter: function Product({ name, price }).
  • Props are read-only: a component must never change its own props.

Worked Example 1

Avoid drilling with composition.

Worked Example 2

Memoized callback prop.

Practice Exercise 1

Props with defaults and a callback.

Practice Exercise 2

TypeScript props.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Props are the first argument of a component function: a frozen plain object. When a parent re-renders, it calls the child with a new props object; the child re-renders unless wrapped in memo and all prop values are shallow-equal (Object.is). Functions and objects created inline have a new identity each render, so they look changed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: destructuring with defaults, rest props (...rest) forwarded to DOM elements, children and render props, passing components as props, the key and ref special props, TypeScript prop types and generics, defaultProps replacement with default parameters, and context for deep data.

expert.content:
Default Props and the Prop-Drilling Problem

Default values can be given via default parameters in the destructuring, so a component still works sensibly even if a prop is omitted.

Prop drilling is what happens when a deeply nested component needs a prop, forcing every intermediate component in between to accept and re-pass it, even if they don't use it themselves. It's a real maintenance pain in larger apps — the standard fix is the Context API (covered separately), which lets data skip levels directly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Can a child component modify the props it receives?No — props are read-only from the child's perspective; only the parent that owns the data can change it (typically triggering it to re-render and pass new prop values down)
What is "one-way data flow" in React?Data flows from parent to child via props only, never the reverse directly - a child that needs to affect the parent does so via a callback function passed down as a prop
What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?Passing a prop through many intermediate components that don't use it, just to reach a deeply nested child - solved with the Context API for widely-needed data

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pass any value: strings, numbers, objects, arrays and functions (callbacks).
  • Default values with destructuring: ({ qty = 1 }).
  • The special children prop holds nested content.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid prop drilling (passing through many levels) with composition, context or state libraries.
  • Pass stable references (memoized callbacks and objects) to memoized children to avoid needless re-renders.
  • Validate props with TypeScript types (or PropTypes) to document and check the contract.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mutating props, copying props into state, passing too many props (a sign of poor boundaries), unstable object/function props to memoized children, and forgetting required props. Pass fewer, more meaningful props and use TypeScript.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

To keep memoized children effective, stabilize props with useMemo/useCallback or move the creation of constants outside the component. Do this only after measuring, since memoization has its own cost.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a data table component with a flexible API. Columns are configuration props, cell renderers are functions, and callbacks report sorting and selection to the parent.
codeExamples:
<DataTable rows={orders} columns={[{ key: "id", header: "#" }, { key: "total", header: "Total", render: o => "₹" + o.total.toFixed(2) }]} sort={sort} onSortChange={setSort} onRowClick={o => navigate("/orders/" + o.id)} />

// OUTPUT:
// a sortable table; clicking a row navigates to the order page

beginner.content:
What is State?

• State is data that belongs to a component and can change over time — unlike props, state is owned and managed BY the component itself, not passed in from outside.
• When state changes, React automatically re-renders the component to reflect the new value on screen.
• The useState Hook is how a functional component declares state.

Never Mutate State Directly

Calling setCount(...) is what tells React "re-render me" — directly assigning to a state variable (count = count + 1) is actually a hard TypeError, because count is declared with const. The subtler trap is MUTATING an object or array already in state (user.name = "x"), which runs fine but keeps the same reference, so React does NOT trigger a re-render and leaves React's internal tracking out of sync with reality.

Fresher Notes

  • State is data that changes over time and makes the component re-render. const [value, setValue] = useState(initial).
  • Call the setter to update: setCount(count + 1). Never change state directly.
  • Each component instance has its own state.

Worked Example 1

Derived value instead of state.

Worked Example 2

useReducer.

Practice Exercise 1

Counters and functional updates.

Practice Exercise 2

Immutable list updates.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

useState stores a value in the component fiber, in the slot matching the call order. The setter does not change the current variable: it enqueues an update and schedules a re-render, in which the function runs again and useState returns the new value. Several updates in one event are batched. If the new value is identical (Object.is), React skips re-rendering.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: useState(initial), lazy initializer useState(() => read()), functional updates, object/array state with copies, useReducer, useRef for mutable values that do not trigger renders, useSyncExternalStore for external stores, useDeferredValue and useTransition for non-urgent updates.

expert.content:
State vs Props

AspectPropsState
Owned byParent component (passed down)The component itself
MutabilityRead-only from the receiving componentMutable, but ONLY via its setter function
Triggers re-render?Yes, when the parent's prop value changesYes, when the setter is called with a new value
PurposeConfigure/customize a component from outsideTrack data that changes over the component's lifetime

Functional Updates for State Based on Previous State

When the new state depends on the old state, pass a function to the setter instead of a plain value — this avoids subtle bugs from stale values in fast-firing updates (e.g. multiple rapid clicks).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What happens if you mutate state directly instead of using the setter?The component does NOT re-render, because React only knows to update the UI when the state setter function is called
Why use the functional form setCount(prev => prev + 1) instead of setCount(count + 1)?It guarantees you're updating from the truly latest state, avoiding stale-closure bugs when multiple updates happen close together
Does calling the state setter update the variable immediately?No - state updates are asynchronous/batched; the component re-renders with the new value on the NEXT render, not synchronously in the same line of code

Mid-Level Notes

  • State updates are batched and applied for the next render; the old value is still visible in the current function.
  • Use the functional form when the new value depends on the old: setCount(c => c + 1).
  • For objects and arrays create new copies (spread, map, filter) instead of mutating.

Senior Notes

  • Keep state minimal: derive values during render instead of storing duplicates.
  • Lift state up to the nearest common parent when siblings need it; use context or a store for wide sharing.
  • useReducer suits complex state transitions; lazy initial state useState(() => compute()) avoids repeated expensive initialization.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mutating state (push, direct assignment), relying on the value right after setState, storing derived data, using index-based ids, and putting everything in one giant state object. Update immutably, use functional updates, derive values and split state.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

State placement affects performance: state held high re-renders the whole subtree. Keep state close to where it is used, split large objects, and use context selectors or stores (Zustand, Redux) for widely shared fast-changing state.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a multi-step form wizard. A reducer holds the step and data, validation runs per step, and the final submission sends the combined data.

beginner.content:
Handling Events in React

• React events are named using camelCase (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) rather than lowercase HTML attribute names.
• You pass a function as the handler, not a string of code — onClick={handleClick}, not onClick="handleClick()".
• React wraps native browser events in a SyntheticEvent — a cross-browser wrapper that behaves consistently no matter which browser is running the code.
Handling Form Input with onChange

Fresher Notes

  • Handle events with props like onClick, onChange, onSubmit, passing a function: <button onClick={save}>.
  • Pass the function itself, do not call it: onClick={save}, not onClick={save()}.
  • The handler receives a synthetic event object with target and preventDefault().

Worked Example 1

Common bug.
codeExamples:
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Save</button>      // runs on render
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>        // runs on click

// OUTPUT:
// the first form triggers an infinite re-render loop if handleClick sets state

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Debounced search effect.

Practice Exercise 1

Handlers with state.

Practice Exercise 2

Passing arguments.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

React attaches one listener per event type to the root container and dispatches synthetic events to your handlers following the component tree (capture then bubble). Handlers run inside React's batching, so state updates made in one event cause one re-render. The synthetic event wraps the native event and normalizes behaviour across browsers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Handler forms: inline arrows, named functions, handlers created by factory functions (onChange={handle("name")}), event delegation by data- attributes, refs and native listeners for non-React events, useEffectEvent (new) for stable event callbacks in effects, and async handlers with loading state.

expert.content:
Passing Arguments to Event Handlers

To pass extra arguments to a handler, wrap the call in an inline arrow function — calling the function directly (onClick={handleClick(id)}) would invoke it immediately during render, not on click.

preventDefault() in Forms

By default, submitting an HTML form reloads the page — call event.preventDefault() inside the submit handler to stop that and handle the submission entirely in JavaScript/React.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a SyntheticEvent?React's cross-browser wrapper around the native DOM event, providing a consistent API regardless of which browser fires the underlying event
Why does onClick={handleClick(id)} fire immediately instead of on click?Writing it with parentheses CALLS the function during render and uses its return value as the handler, instead of passing the function itself - wrap it in an arrow function to defer the call
What does event.preventDefault() do in a form's onSubmit handler?Stops the browser's default full-page reload/navigation so the form can be handled entirely in JavaScript

Mid-Level Notes

  • To pass arguments, wrap: onClick={() => remove(id)}.
  • Prevent form reloads with e.preventDefault() in onSubmit.
  • Event handlers can update state; avoid heavy work inside them or move it to async functions.

Senior Notes

  • React attaches events at the root and delegates; handlers run in the same batch as state updates.
  • Avoid creating many inline handlers in huge lists when it hurts performance; use delegation or memoized items.
  • Debounce or throttle expensive handlers (search, resize) with a timer or library.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: calling the handler during render, losing this in class components, stale values in handlers (closures over old state), async handlers without error handling, and attaching document listeners without cleanup. Use functional updates, try/catch/finally and effect cleanup.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Frequent events (mousemove, scroll, input) can flood renders. Throttle, debounce, use passive listeners, move heavy work off the handler (startTransition, workers) and avoid state updates for values that need no re-render (use refs).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a keyboard-accessible autocomplete. Arrow keys move the highlighted option, Enter selects, Escape closes, and focus and ARIA attributes stay in sync.

beginner.content:
Ways to Render Conditionally in React

JSX doesn't allow if statements directly inside curly braces (only expressions), so React code uses a few standard patterns to show different UI based on a condition.

1. if/else Outside the JSX

2. Ternary Operator Inside JSX

Good for a simple either/or choice embedded directly in the markup.

Fresher Notes

  • Conditional rendering shows different UI depending on state or props, using normal JavaScript.
  • Options: if with early return, the ternary cond ? <A /> : <B />, and cond && <A />.
  • Returning null renders nothing.

Worked Example 1

Zero pitfall.

Worked Example 2

Role based UI.

Practice Exercise 1

Loading, error, empty and data states.

Practice Exercise 2

Toggle with state.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Conditional rendering is ordinary JavaScript producing different element trees. During reconciliation React compares the new tree with the previous one: if the element type and position are the same, the existing instance (with its state) is reused; if the type or key differs, the old subtree is unmounted and a new one is mounted. null, undefined, true and false render nothing.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: early returns for loading/error/empty, ternary for two branches, && for optional pieces, switch or lookup objects for many cases, component maps (const views = { list: List, grid: Grid }), Suspense fallback for async parts, and hidden/CSS for keeping state while hiding.

expert.content:
3. && Short-Circuit Rendering

For "render something only if true, otherwise render nothing," the && operator is a common shorthand — JSX treats false/null/undefined as "render nothing."

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't you write "if" directly inside JSX curly braces?Curly braces in JSX only accept expressions (things that evaluate to a value), and "if" is a statement, not an expression
What does React render for false, null, or undefined?Nothing - React silently skips rendering these values, which is why they're used as the "render nothing" branch of conditional patterns
What's the "renders a literal 0" bug with && and how do you avoid it?count &&

...

renders the number 0 on screen when count is 0, because 0 is a "falsy but rendered" value in React unlike false/null/undefined - fix by using a comparison like count > 0 && ... instead

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use && carefully: {count && <X />} prints 0 when count is 0; use count > 0 &&.
  • Extract complex conditions into variables or small components for readability.
  • Toggle visibility with state (useState(false)) and a button handler.

Senior Notes

  • Rendering different component types resets state; rendering the same type in the same position keeps it.
  • Hiding with CSS keeps the component mounted (and its state); conditional rendering unmounts it.
  • Handle loading, error and empty states explicitly for a good user experience.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: the 0 rendering bug, deeply nested ternaries, forgetting loading and error states (flicker or blank screens), conditionally calling hooks (not allowed), and relying on conditional rendering for security (a hidden button is still client code). Keep conditions flat and hooks unconditional.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Unmounting and remounting expensive components is costly. Keep heavy tabs mounted but hidden when switching is frequent, and lazy-mount them on first use. Use Suspense and lazy to defer code for rarely shown branches.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: feature flags and permissions. A small component hides UI for features that are off, while the server independently enforces access.

beginner.content:
Rendering Lists with .map()

React doesn't have a special "for loop" syntax in JSX. Instead, you transform an array of data into an array of JSX elements using the standard JavaScript .map() method, and React renders each element in the resulting array.

Why Keys Are Required

• React uses a reconciliation (diffing) algorithm to figure out what changed between renders, so it only touches the real DOM where necessary.
• A key is a special prop that gives each list item a stable identity across renders, so React can tell "this item moved" apart from "this item was deleted and a new one was added".
• Without keys (or with unstable keys), React may re-render, re-mount, or mismatch list items incorrectly - especially when items are reordered, inserted, or removed.

Fresher Notes

  • Render lists with array.map() and return an element for each item.
  • Each element in a list needs a unique key prop: <li key={item.id}>.
  • Keys help React match items between renders so it updates, moves and removes the right DOM nodes.

Worked Example 1

Virtualized list.
codeExamples:
{({ index, style }) =>
{rows[index].name}
} // OUTPUT: // 100,000 rows with about 15 DOM nodes

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Group and render sections.

Practice Exercise 1

Keyed list with sorting.

Practice Exercise 2

The index key bug.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Reconciliation of children lists uses keys: React builds a map of the previous children by key and matches new children against it. A matching key keeps the same component instance (and DOM node), so state and focus move with the item; new keys mount new instances, missing keys unmount. Without keys React falls back to index matching.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Key sources: database ids, UUIDs created when the item is created (not during render), natural unique values, composite keys (type + "-" + id). Fragments with keys group multiple elements per item. Changing a component key deliberately resets its state (a common reset technique).

expert.content:
The Index-as-Key Trap

Using the array index as the key (key={index}) works fine ONLY if the list is static and never reordered/filtered/has items inserted in the middle. The moment the list changes shape, index-as-key causes React to associate the wrong internal state with the wrong visual item - a classic, hard-to-spot bug.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does React need a key prop for list items?So its reconciliation algorithm can track each item's identity across re-renders, correctly distinguishing "moved" from "added" from "removed"
Why is using the array index as key discouraged?If the list can be reordered, filtered, or have items inserted/removed anywhere but the end, index-as-key causes React to misattribute state/DOM to the wrong item
When is index-as-key actually safe?Only for a static list that never changes order and is never filtered or has items inserted/removed
Do keys need to be globally unique across the whole app?No - only unique among siblings within the same list

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use stable, unique ids from the data as keys; avoid array indexes when the list can be reordered, filtered or edited.
  • Keys only need to be unique among siblings, and they are not passed as props.
  • Missing or duplicate keys trigger a warning and can cause wrong state or UI bugs.

Senior Notes

  • Using index as key with inputs or stateful items makes state stick to positions, not items, after reordering.
  • Generate ids when data is created (not during render with Math.random).
  • For long lists use virtualization (react-window, TanStack Virtual) so only visible rows render.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: Math.random() or Date.now() as keys during render (remount every time), duplicate keys, keys on the wrong element (they must be on the outermost element returned by map), index keys with reordering, and large lists without virtualization. Generate stable ids at data creation.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Updating one item in a long list re-renders the list; memoize rows and keep their props stable. Virtualize lists beyond a few hundred rows and paginate or infinite-scroll data from the server.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a sortable, filterable table with stable keys, memoized rows, a virtualized body and server-side pagination.

beginner.content:
Controlled Components

A controlled component is a form input whose value is driven entirely by React state - the input's value comes from state, and every keystroke fires an onChange handler that updates that state. This makes React the single source of truth for the form's data.

Fresher Notes

  • A controlled input has its value held in state: <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />.
  • Handle submit with onSubmit and call e.preventDefault().
  • For many fields keep an object in state and update with a generic handler.

Worked Example 1

React Hook Form with Zod.

Worked Example 2

Checkbox and select.
codeExamples:
<input type="checkbox" checked={agree} onChange={e => setAgree(e.target.checked)} />
<select value={country} onChange={e => setCountry(e.target.value)}><option value="IN">India</option><option value="US">USA</option></select>

// OUTPUT:
// state holds true/false and the selected value

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Controlled form with validation.

Practice Exercise 2

Uncontrolled with FormData.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In a controlled form every keystroke calls onChange, which sets state and re-renders the component, so the input value always equals state. React sets the DOM value from state on each render. Uncontrolled inputs keep their value in the DOM; you read it on demand through refs or FormData. A form submit triggers onSubmit where you validate and send data.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: one change handler with name attributes, nested state updates, derived validation, async validation with debounce, file inputs (e.target.files), useActionState and form actions (React 19), schema validation (Zod/Yup), React Hook Form (register, handleSubmit, watch), and optimistic UI for submissions.

expert.content:
Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

An uncontrolled component lets the DOM itself hold the input's value, and React reads it on demand via a ref instead of tracking every keystroke in state. Controlled components are the React-recommended default (predictable, easy to validate/format as the user types); uncontrolled components are occasionally useful for simple forms or integrating non-React code.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a controlled component?A form input whose value is driven by React state, updated via an onChange handler on every change
What is an uncontrolled component?A form input where the DOM holds the current value; React reads it on demand via a ref instead of tracking it in state
Why call e.preventDefault() in a form's onSubmit handler?To stop the browser's default full-page-reload form submission, since React handles the submission in JavaScript instead
Which approach is generally recommended in React?Controlled components, since they keep React as the single source of truth and make validation/conditional logic straightforward

Mid-Level Notes

  • Different controls: value for text and select, checked for checkboxes, onChange for all.
  • Uncontrolled inputs use refs or FormData and read values on submit; they are simpler for large forms.
  • Validate on submit and on blur; show clear errors near fields and link them with aria attributes.

Senior Notes

  • Use libraries (React Hook Form, Formik) with schema validation (Zod, Yup) for complex forms; they reduce re-renders.
  • Server actions and form libraries handle submission state (pending, errors); always validate again on the server.
  • Accessibility: labels, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, focus the first invalid field.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: switching between controlled and uncontrolled (value undefined to defined warning), forgetting preventDefault, storing numbers as strings and comparing wrongly, no labels, not disabling the button during submit (double submit), and only validating on the client. Initialize state with empty strings and validate on the server too.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large controlled forms re-render fully on each keystroke. Split into field components with local state, use React Hook Form (uncontrolled), or debounce expensive validation. Measure with the Profiler.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a checkout form with client validation, accessible error messages, a disabled submit while pending, idempotency on the server and focus on the first error.

beginner.content:
What is a Side Effect?

A side effect is anything a component does besides computing what to render - fetching data from an API, setting up a subscription, manually touching the DOM, or logging. The useEffect hook is where side effects belong in a functional component, kept separate from the render logic itself.

useEffect Syntax

useEffect(() => { ...effect code... }, [dependencies]) - the function runs after render, and the dependency array controls WHEN it runs again.

Fresher Notes

  • useEffect runs code after the component renders, for side effects such as fetching data, timers and subscriptions.
  • The dependency array controls when it runs: [] once after mount, [a] when a changes, none after every render.
  • Return a cleanup function to remove timers or subscriptions.

Worked Example 1

Derived value, no effect needed.

Worked Example 2

Stale closure fix.

Practice Exercise 1

Fetch with cleanup.

Practice Exercise 2

Subscription and timer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

After React commits a render, it runs effects whose dependencies changed since the previous render (compared with Object.is). Before running an effect again, it runs the previous effect's cleanup. On unmount all cleanups run. Effects see the props and state of the render they belong to (closures), which is why dependencies matter.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Related hooks and patterns: useLayoutEffect, useInsertionEffect, useSyncExternalStore (subscribe to stores), useEvent-style callbacks, custom hooks (useFetch, useLocalStorage, useDebounce), and libraries for server state (TanStack Query, SWR).

expert.content:
The Dependency Array's Three Behaviors

Dependency arrayWhen the effect runs
Omitted entirelyAfter every single render (rarely what you want)
[] (empty)Once, right after the first render (mount) only
[dep1, dep2]After the first render, then again whenever any listed dependency's value changes

Cleanup Functions

If your effect sets up something that needs tearing down (a subscription, a timer, an event listener), return a cleanup function from the effect - React calls it right before the effect re-runs, and again when the component unmounts.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a side effect in React?Anything a component does outside computing its render output - data fetching, subscriptions, timers, manual DOM access, logging
What does an empty dependency array [] mean?The effect runs exactly once, right after the component's first render (similar in spirit to componentDidMount)
Why return a function from useEffect?To define a cleanup step that runs before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts, preventing leaks (e.g. clearing intervals/subscriptions)
What happens if you omit the dependency array entirely?The effect runs after every render, which is rarely intended and can cause performance issues or infinite loops if it also updates state

Mid-Level Notes

  • Include every reactive value used inside the effect in the dependency array (the lint rule helps).
  • Do not use effects to derive data from props or state: compute it during render.
  • Fetch effects need cancellation or an ignore flag to avoid setting state after unmount or from stale requests.

Senior Notes

  • Effects are for synchronizing with external systems; many uses (derived state, event responses) do not need an effect.
  • In Strict Mode (development) effects run twice on mount to reveal missing cleanup.
  • Prefer data libraries (TanStack Query, SWR) over hand-written fetch effects for caching, retries and deduplication.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: missing dependencies (stale values), object or function dependencies that change every render (effect runs constantly), effects that set state causing loops, fetching without cancellation (race conditions), and using effects for things that belong in event handlers or render. Follow the exhaustive-deps lint rule.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Too many effects and re-runs cost time. Remove unnecessary effects, memoize object dependencies, batch updates, and use query libraries to cache and deduplicate requests. Check how often effects run with the Profiler and console logs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: live data. An effect opens a WebSocket for a room, handles messages with the latest handler via a ref, and closes the connection in cleanup when the room changes.

beginner.content:
The Problem: Prop Drilling

Prop drilling is passing a prop down through several layers of components that don't actually use it themselves, just to get it to a deeply nested child that does. It clutters every intermediate component's props and makes refactoring painful.

The Fix: Context API

Context lets you share a value (theme, logged-in user, language setting, etc.) across a whole subtree of components WITHOUT passing it through every intermediate level as a prop.

Fresher Notes

  • Context shares data with many components without passing props through every level (prop drilling).
  • Create with createContext, provide with <Context.Provider value={...}>, read with useContext(Context).
  • Typical uses: theme, current user, language.

Worked Example 1

Split state and dispatch contexts.

Worked Example 2

Zustand alternative.

Practice Exercise 1

Auth context with reducer and custom hook.

Practice Exercise 2

Theme context.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Context stores a value on a Provider in the tree. useContext reads the nearest Provider's value above the component and subscribes the component to it. When the Provider's value changes (Object.is), React re-renders all consumers below it, skipping memoized components that do not consume it. There is no built-in selector, so any change re-renders every consumer.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Good practice: memoize provider values, split state and actions into separate contexts, create a custom hook with a guard, keep providers near where needed, combine with useReducer, and consider selector-based libraries (Zustand, Jotai, Redux) for fast-changing shared state. Default values are used when there is no provider.

expert.content:
When Context Is (and Isn't) the Right Tool

• Good fit: values needed by MANY components at different nesting depths (theme, auth/current-user, locale, feature flags).
• Overkill: passing a prop just one or two levels down - plain props are simpler and easier to trace.
• Context is not a full state-management replacement for complex, frequently-changing app-wide state - every component consuming a context re-renders when its value changes, which can hurt performance if used carelessly for high-frequency updates.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Context solve?Prop drilling - passing data through many intermediate components that don't need it, just to reach a deeply nested consumer
What are the three pieces of using Context?createContext() to create it, a Provider to supply a value to a subtree, and useContext() to read it in any descendant
Does every component re-render when context changes?Every component that calls useContext() on that context re-renders when its value changes - components that don't consume it are unaffected
Is Context a replacement for Redux/state libraries?Not fully - Context is great for infrequently-changing, widely-needed values, but frequent high-volume updates through Context can cause unnecessary re-renders

Mid-Level Notes

  • Every component that uses the context re-renders when the provider value changes.
  • Keep the value stable (memoize objects) and split contexts by concern (state vs dispatch) to limit re-renders.
  • Provide a custom hook (useAuth()) that wraps useContext and throws if used outside the provider.

Senior Notes

  • Context is not a full state manager; for frequently changing or large state use a store (Zustand, Redux Toolkit) or selectors.
  • Combine with useReducer for predictable updates.
  • Place providers as low as practical so unrelated parts of the tree do not re-render.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: putting everything in one big context, inline object values, using context for rapidly changing values like mouse position, forgetting the provider (silently using the default), and testing without providers. Use focused contexts and a wrapper in tests.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Context update cost scales with the number of consumers. For large trees measure with the Profiler, move rapidly changing state to a store with selectors, or pass values through props to memoized children where the data path is short.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: theming and localization contexts at the root (rarely changing), an auth context with a session refresh, and a small store for the shopping cart.
codeExamples:
<ThemeProvider><I18nProvider locale={locale}><AuthProvider><QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}><App /></QueryClientProvider></AuthProvider></I18nProvider></ThemeProvider>

// OUTPUT:
// stable cross-cutting concerns are available everywhere with no prop drilling

beginner.content:
Client-Side Routing

A Single Page Application has only ONE actual HTML page - "navigating" between "pages" just swaps out which components are rendered, without a full page reload. react-router-dom is the standard library that makes this URL-driven navigation possible in React.

Fresher Notes

  • React Router maps URLs to components so an SPA can have multiple pages without reloads.
  • Set up <BrowserRouter>, define <Routes> with <Route path="/orders" element={...} /> and link with <Link to="/orders">.
  • Read URL parameters with useParams().

Worked Example 1

Data router with loader.

Worked Example 2

Lazy route.

Practice Exercise 1

Routes with a layout and params.

Practice Exercise 2

Programmatic navigation and search params.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The router keeps location state (path, search, hash) in sync with the History API. A matcher ranks route patterns against the path (static segments beat dynamic ones), builds the match tree (parent and child routes), and renders the matching elements nested through Outlet. Link intercepts clicks and calls navigate instead of loading a new document.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features: nested layouts, index routes, dynamic and splat segments, search params, NavLink active styling, useNavigate, Navigate, useLocation, route handle, loaders/actions/deferred data, useFetcher, lazy routes, scroll restoration, and hash or memory routers for special environments.

expert.content:
Dynamic Route Segments with useParams

Routes can include a dynamic segment (like a product id) using a colon prefix (:id). The matching component reads that segment's actual value via the useParams hook.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is client-side routing?Swapping which components render based on the URL, without triggering a full page reload from the server
Difference between Link and a plain <a> tag in React Router?Link intercepts the click and updates the route via JavaScript (no full reload); a plain <a> would trigger a full browser navigation
How do you read a dynamic route segment like /products/:id?The useParams() hook, called inside the component rendered for that route
What wraps the whole app to enable routing?BrowserRouter (or another Router variant), typically at the top of the component tree

Mid-Level Notes

  • Nested routes with <Outlet /> share layouts; NavLink styles the active link; Navigate redirects.
  • Programmatic navigation: const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/orders/42").
  • Query strings: useSearchParams().

Senior Notes

  • Data routers (createBrowserRouter) add loaders, actions and error elements for data fetching and mutations.
  • Lazy load routes with lazy() or route-level lazy for code splitting.
  • Protect routes with a wrapper component, and always enforce authorization on the server.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using plain anchors (full page reload), forgetting the server fallback to index.html, relative path confusion in nested routes, relying on client-side route guards for security, and not handling 404 and error cases. Use Link, a catch-all route and server-enforced authorization.
codeExamples: Orders // full reload Orders // client-side navigation // guard only protects the UI }>} /> // OUTPUT: // the API must also return 403 for non-admin users

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Routing performance: code split per route, prefetch on hover or when links appear (prefetch in frameworks), load data in parallel with code through loaders, and avoid waterfalls (parent waits for data before children start loading).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an e-commerce app with product list and detail routes, URL-based filters (shareable links), a protected account area, and a not-found page.

beginner.content:
The Three Lifecycle Phases

Every component goes through three phases: Mounting (being created and inserted into the DOM for the first time), Updating (re-rendering due to changed props or state), and Unmounting (being removed from the DOM). Class components exposed these phases as named methods; interviewers still ask about them even though functional components + hooks are now the standard.

Fresher Notes

  • A component has a lifecycle: it mounts (is created and added to the page), updates when props or state change, and unmounts (is removed).
  • In function components use useEffect for lifecycle work: mount, update and cleanup on unmount.
  • Class components used methods: componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmount.

Worked Example 1

Measure layout before paint.

Worked Example 2

Error boundary.

Practice Exercise 1

Lifecycle with hooks.

Practice Exercise 2

Class equivalent.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

React works in phases. Render: call components to compute the next tree (pure, may run more than once or be discarded). Commit: apply DOM changes, then run layout effects synchronously, then (after paint) passive effects. For each component: mount runs effects, update re-runs effects whose dependencies changed (after cleanup), unmount runs cleanups.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Class lifecycle methods map to hooks: constructor/state to useState, componentDidMount to useEffect(…, []), componentDidUpdate to useEffect with dependencies, componentWillUnmount to cleanup, getDerivedStateFromProps to deriving during render, shouldComponentUpdate to memo, getSnapshotBeforeUpdate to useLayoutEffect, and error boundaries still need classes.

expert.content:
How useEffect Maps Onto Class Lifecycle Methods

Class lifecycle methodFunctional-component equivalent
componentDidMountuseEffect(() => {...}, []) - empty dependency array
componentDidUpdateuseEffect(() => {...}, [dep1, dep2]) - runs when listed deps change
componentWillUnmountthe cleanup function returned from useEffect

This isn't a perfect 1:1 mapping conceptually (useEffect thinks in terms of "synchronizing with an external system" rather than discrete lifecycle events), but for interview purposes and everyday use, this table captures the practical equivalence.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the three lifecycle phases of a React component?Mounting, Updating, Unmounting
Which class lifecycle method is closest to useEffect(fn, [])?componentDidMount - both run once, right after the component first renders
Where does cleanup logic go in a functional component?In the function returned from useEffect, which React calls before re-running the effect and on unmount
Are class components still relevant to learn?Mostly for reading legacy code and interviews - new code overwhelmingly uses functional components with hooks

Mid-Level Notes

  • Mapping: useEffect(fn, []) is like componentDidMount (and its cleanup like componentWillUnmount); useEffect(fn, [dep]) like componentDidUpdate for dep.
  • Render phase must be pure; effects run after the browser paints (use useLayoutEffect to run before paint).
  • Strict Mode double-invokes render and effects in development to surface impure code.

Senior Notes

  • Think in synchronization, not lifecycle: an effect describes how to sync with something for given values, and cleanup how to stop.
  • Error boundaries (class components) catch render errors in the subtree; there is no hook version yet.
  • Concurrent features (Suspense, transitions) can render components that are never committed, so render must have no side effects.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: side effects in render, forgetting cleanup (leaks, duplicate listeners), assuming effects run once (Strict Mode runs them twice in development), reading stale props in async callbacks, and updating state after unmount. Write idempotent effects with cleanup.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Lifecycle cost shows up as slow mounts (heavy initialization), expensive effects after every render, and layout effects that block paint. Defer non-critical work (requestIdleCallback, useDeferredValue), lazy initialize state and keep layout effects tiny.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a component that tracks page views and focus. It sends an analytics event on mount and route change, pauses a video on unmount, and flushes pending data when the tab becomes hidden.

cheatNotes: ReactJS - JavaScript library for building component-based user interfaces
JSX - Syntax extension letting you write HTML-like markup in JavaScript
Component - Reusable, self-contained piece of UI
Functional component - Component written as a plain JS function
Class component - Component written as an ES6 class extending React.Component
Props - Read-only data passed from parent to child component
State - Mutable data local to a component, triggers re-render on change
Props vs State - Props are external/immutable, state is internal/mutable
useState - Hook to add state to a functional component
useEffect - Hook to run side effects after render (data fetching, subscriptions)
useEffect cleanup - Return a function from useEffect to clean up on unmount
Dependency array - Controls when useEffect re-runs
useRef - Hook to persist a mutable value/DOM reference without re-rendering
useContext - Hook to consume a Context value without prop drilling
useMemo - Hook to memoize expensive computed values
useCallback - Hook to memoize function references between renders
Custom hooks - Reusable functions starting with 'use' that encapsulate hook logic
Component lifecycle - Mounting, updating, unmounting phases
componentDidMount/Update/WillUnmount - Class component lifecycle methods
Conditional rendering - Rendering JSX based on conditions (ternary, &&, if)
Lists & keys - key prop helps React identify changed/added/removed list items
Event handling - Attaching handlers like onClick, onChange in JSX using camelCase
Controlled component - Form input value driven by React state
Uncontrolled component - Form input value managed by the DOM itself (via ref)
Lifting state up - Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor
Context API - Share data across component tree without passing props manually
Virtual DOM - In-memory representation of the real DOM for efficient updates
Reconciliation - React's diffing algorithm to update only changed DOM nodes
React.memo - Higher-order component that memoizes a component to avoid re-renders
React Router - Library for client-side routing/navigation in React apps
<Routes>/<Route> - Define URL paths and matching components
useNavigate - Hook to programmatically navigate between routes
useParams - Hook to read dynamic route parameters
Fragments (<>...</>) - Group elements without adding extra DOM nodes
Prop drilling - Passing props through many nested levels of components
SPA - Single Page Application, updates content without full page reload
